stem: A new irregular radial pulse is found. Which assessment avoids undercounting the rate?

options.text: Count apically for a full minute
options.why: A radial count can undercount an irregular pulse.
The radial count can undercount.
The lecture calls for manual assessment.
A new irregular pulse must be reported.

explanation: A radial count can undercount an irregular pulse.

stem: Urine output falls in a cardiac patient. Which check helps interpret this finding?

options.text: Check catheter patency and fluid-balance accuracy
options.why: Both checks are specified.
Congestion is another possible cause.
The cause may be fluid overload.
Persistent low output needs urgent review.

stem: New unilateral leg swelling with warmth suggests what next assessment?

options.why: Unilateral warmth or calf pain needs a DVT assessment.
Bilateral dependent oedema better fits cardiac oedema.
Pattern and other findings also matter.
New oedema is always reported.

explanation: Unilateral warmth or calf pain needs a DVT assessment.

stem: A cardiac patient develops a postural BP drop. What should be checked?

options.text: Repeat manual lying and standing BP and assess pulse, consciousness, fluid balance and bleeding
options.why: These are specified checks.
Weight omits the stated checks.
Bleeding and arrhythmia are also possible.
A new drop must be reported.

stem: SpO₂ stays stable but oxygen requirement rises. What does the trend mean?

options.why: The lecture explicitly identifies stable saturations on more oxygen as deterioration.
Oxygen need has risen.
Trends can show slow deterioration.
The observation chart includes oxygen need.

explanation: The lecture explicitly identifies stable saturations on more oxygen as deterioration.

stem: Chest pain persists after a normal first ECG. What next?

options.why: One normal ECG does not exclude ACS.
The first ECG cannot exclude it.
The lecture says not to wait.
Full vital signs are part of the response.

explanation: One normal ECG does not exclude ACS.

stem: Bleeding starts at a groin access site after PCI. What is the immediate response?

options.text: Apply direct pressure above the puncture and have someone call for help
options.why: This is the stated response.
Urgent review is required every time.

options.text: Check only the next routine pulse
options.why: Distal pulses and vital signs are needed now.
Bleeding requires immediate action.

stem: Forearm pain, swelling and tightness increase after radial PCI. What next?

options.why: These are signs of compartment syndrome.
The source explicitly rejects waiting.
These are warning signs.
The radial limb needs assessment.

explanation: These are signs of compartment syndrome.

stem: A standard wrist site is unavailable for a diagnostic ECG. What placement is advised?

options.text: Use the most distal available limb point, mirror it contralaterally and document it
options.why: The page specifies this modification.

options.text: Move leads to the torso without documentation
options.why: Torso placement alters morphology.
Symmetry is recommended.
Modified limb placement is described.
This is V3.

options.text: Right sternal margin, fourth intercostal space
options.why: This is V1.

options.text: Left sternal margin, fourth intercostal space
options.why: This is V2.
This is V6.

stem: Lead II is predominantly downward and aVR upright. What quality issue should be checked?

options.why: The source describes reversal of these waveform directions.
Normally II is upright and aVR downward.

options.text: Diagnose a rhythm from this alone
options.why: Misplacement can cause diagnostic error.
Electrode position needs checking.

explanation: The source describes reversal of these waveform directions.

stem: An ECG baseline is bumpy and spiky while the patient shivers. Likely cause?

options.why: Shivering can produce this artefact.
That produces a dotted baseline.
That reverses waveform direction.
A good baseline is sharp and flat.

stem: One ECG lead shows a dotted baseline. What should be checked?

options.why: A missing lead indicates failed conduction.
This can cause a wandering baseline.
The lead is missing.
Talking causes muscle artefact.

explanation: A missing lead indicates failed conduction.

stem: Monitoring shows a rhythm change. What records a specific diagnostic tracing?

options.why: Monitoring watches rhythm but does not diagnose.
It is surveillance, not diagnostic ECG.
It changes transmission method.
Disconnection loses surveillance.

explanation: Monitoring watches rhythm but does not diagnose.

stem: A high-risk patient on hardwire cardiac monitoring needs to get to the toilet. What does the Canvas monitoring page tell you to plan?

options.text: How toileting and transfers will be managed: supervision, a commode at the bedside, or a switch to telemetry if they are mobile enough
options.why: The page says to think ahead about toileting and transfers for a high-risk patient, because every disconnection is a period when the rhythm is not being watched.

options.text: Nothing: hardwire monitoring lets the patient walk around the ward
options.why: Hardwire monitoring limits movement to cable reach; the patient must be disconnected to leave the bedspace. Walking around the ward is what telemetry allows.

options.text: Record a 12-lead ECG instead of monitoring while they are up
options.why: The page says a 12-lead ECG is recorded when a diagnosis is needed; it is not a substitute for watching the rhythm during mobility.

options.text: Turn off the monitor alarms until they return
options.why: The page describes alarms as how staff are alerted to rhythm changes; it does not suggest turning them off.

explanation: Hardwire: cable to a bedside monitor, so movement is limited. Telemetry: a wireless transmitter the patient carries, so they can walk around the ward. Each disconnection from hardwire is unwatched time.

stem: Where is medication added to the described burette?

options.why: The instruction specifies this site.
Medication must not go through the vent.
Needles and blunt cannulae are prohibited there.
This prevents air entering the line.

prompt: A new fast, irregular pulse is found with breathlessness. Outline the assessment and escalation.
model: Check pulse and BP. Assess radial rate, rhythm and volume manually; if irregular, count apically for a full minute. Check BP, conscious state, 12-lead ECG and cardiac monitoring. Tell the nurse in charge, document, and seek immediate urgent review because of breathlessness.

rubric.point: Manual pulse and full-minute apical count if irregular
BP, conscious state, ECG and monitoring

prompt: A tracing has a dotted baseline in one lead. Explain likely causes and checks before interpretation.
model: A dotted missing-lead baseline indicates failed conduction from skin to monitor. Check skin preparation, electrode gel and contact, cable tension, peeling electrodes, and damaged wires.

rubric.point: Checks skin preparation and electrode contact
Checks dry electrodes, cable tension and damaged wires

prompt: Explain how to prime the administration line and why to keep the burette vertical.
model: Use burette fluid to prime the administration line until all air is removed, then close the lower clamp. Keep the chamber vertical so the floating safety shut-off valve can function and prevent air entering the line when it empties.

rubric.point: Primes with burette fluid and removes all air
Keeps chamber vertical for floating valve function

prompt: After PCI, what access-site and distal limb checks are needed, and what findings need immediate escalation?
model: Check the access site and band for bleeding. Compare distal colour, warmth, movement, sensation and pulses with baseline. Escalate increasing forearm pain, swelling or tightness immediately. Back or flank pain with hypotension suggests retroperitoneal bleeding; new chest pain needs ECG and escalation.

rubric.point: Compares distal neurovascular findings with baseline
Escalates radial forearm pain, swelling or tightness
Recognises back or flank pain with hypotension and new chest pain
